title: Data structures, side by side.
lead: Short explanations, honest complexity comparisons, and step-by-step graphics you can move through at your own pace.

title: Operation costs at a glance
lead: Compare the same operation under the same assumptions. A fast minimum lookup is not a fast arbitrary-key search.

title: Binary heap
lead: A compact priority queue. The smallest value stays at the root, while the array stays complete.

title: d-ary heap
lead: Give each parent more children to shorten the tree. Removal then compares more children at each level.

title: Winner tree
lead: Treat records as players. Each internal match remembers its winner, so the root identifies the next record to output.

title: Loser tree
lead: Each match stores the loser. The overall winner is kept separately, ready to replay against remembered opponents.

title: Huffman tree
lead: Combine the two lightest trees repeatedly. Frequent symbols end up with short codes, and small runs get merged first.

title: Dual min/max heaps
lead: Keep every record twice: once in a min heap and once in a max heap. Cross-pointers keep the copies synchronized.

title: Correspondence heaps
lead: Split records between a min queue and a max queue, with ordered pairs between them and one buffer for an odd item.

title: Interval heap
lead: Store a small interval at every node. The low endpoints form a min heap and the high endpoints form a max heap.

title: Leftist tree
lead: Keep the right spine short. Meld walks along right spines and repairs the leftist rule on the way back.

title: Lazy binomial heap
lead: Add roots cheaply. During removeMin, combine equal-degree trees like carrying digits in binary addition.

title: Fibonacci heap
lead: Use a loose forest and marks to make priority improvements cheap over a sequence. Consolidate when removing an extreme.

title: Pairing heap
lead: Keep one heap-ordered tree. Compare-link makes meld simple, while two-pass pairing makes removal efficient over a sequence.

title: Hash table
lead: Compute a bucket from the key. Fast exact lookup is the strength; sorted order is not maintained.

title: Binary search tree
lead: Keys smaller than a node go left; larger keys go right. All ordered operations follow from that rule.

title: Indexed BST
lead: Add leftSize to each node, so the tree can answer “which item is at rank k?” without traversing all earlier items.

title: Optimal BST
lead: For a fixed dictionary with known access frequencies, choose a shape that minimizes expected search comparisons.

title: AVL tree
lead: Keep the two subtree heights within one at every node. Rotations restore that rule while preserving sorted order.

title: Red-black tree
lead: Color constraints limit height while allowing more flexibility than AVL. Repairs use recoloring and rotations.

title: B-tree
lead: Store many ordered keys in one node to reduce disk or cache accesses. Split overfull nodes; repair underfull ones by borrowing or merging.

title: 2-3 tree
lead: The smallest useful B-tree: every data node holds one or two keys, and all leaf levels agree.

title: 2-3-4 tree
lead: Allow one more key per node. Red-black trees can represent the same degree-balanced idea using colored binary links.

title: B+ tree
lead: Keep all records at the leaves, link those leaves, and use internal keys only to route searches.

title: Splay tree
lead: After access, rotate the relevant node to the root. Frequently used regions tend to stay easy to reach.

title: Digital search tree
lead: Store a whole record at every node, but use successive key bits to choose branches.

title: Binary trie
lead: Branch nodes inspect bits; element nodes hold records. A lookup makes at most one full-key comparison at its candidate leaf.

title: Compressed binary trie
lead: Skip bit positions where all remaining keys agree. Store the next meaningful bit number at each branch.

title: Higher-order trie
lead: Use a digit or a group of digits per branch. Larger fanout reduces height but leaves more pointer slots to store.

title: Multibit trie and routing
lead: Consume several address bits per node, while remembering the most specific matching routing prefix.

title: Suffix tree
lead: Index every suffix of a source string. A substring query becomes a prefix search through those suffixes.

title: Operation names and exam traps
lead: Different names often describe the same repair. Similar names can also hide different assumptions.

title: External sorting
lead: Make sorted runs that fit in memory, then merge them. Count disk transfers before counting comparisons.

title: Amortized analysis
lead: Bound total cost across a sequence, using earlier cheap operations to pay for later expensive ones without assuming random inputs.
